definition: Individual Retirement Accounts (IRAs) are personal retirement savings accounts that offer tax benefits similar to those of employer-sponsored plans, like 401k plans. They can be opened through banks or investment firms, and offer a broader range of investment options than many employer-controlled plans. An employee can contribute up to a certain amount each year set by the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) that does not incur taxes until the person withdraws the money from the account. For 2025, contributions are limited to $7,000 per year ($8,000 if age 50 or older). Traditional IRA contributions may be tax-deductible depending on income and workplace retirement plan coverage. Withdrawals are taxed as income, with a 10% penalty before age 59½ unless an exception applies. Required minimum distributions must begin at age 73. Roth IRAs use after-tax contributions, allow tax-free withdrawals in retirement, and have no required minimum distributions. Eligibility phases out for higher incomes (in 2025, single filers above about $150,000 and joint filers above about $236,000).
